transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I guess what finally made me come in is… I’m having a harder time keeping all the moving parts organized. It’s probably not a huge crisis, but between patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, and team decisions, I keep finding myself just starting whatever is loudest or most urgent-feeling, instead of what actually matters most. And it’s been getting a bit… messy, I suppose.
Do you find it difficult to stay organized or focused on tasks outside of work, like managing household responsibilities or following through with personal commitments?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, because I do eventually get things done, but lately even outside of “pure work” stuff, it feels like there are too many moving pieces in my head.

What pushed me to come in was that I can’t seem to organize all of it very well anymore—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and I end up starting whatever feels loudest or most urgent, instead of what probably matters most. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing you mean.
Can you describe how you manage routine tasks like grocery shopping, paying bills, or keeping track of appointments? Do you find yourself forgetting things or losing track of what needs to be done?

I try to keep lists and reminders, and I can usually make it work, but… honestly, what’s been happening is that I don’t seem to organize the moving parts very well anymore. It’s not just one thing, it’s like patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—all sitting in my head at once.

And then instead of calmly figuring out what actually matters most, I’ll start with whatever feels loudest or most urgent in the moment. I know that’s maybe not exactly grocery shopping or bills, but it’s the same kind of tracking problem, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed that you're having more trouble getting started on tasks or following them through, even when you know they need to be done?

Yes… I think that’s fair. I don’t know if I’d say I’m completely unable to start things, because I do start things, but I’m not starting them in a very sensible order.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and I’ll end up jumping into whatever feels loudest or most urgent, rather than what actually matters most. And then the follow-through gets messy because I’ve started the wrong thing first, if that makes sense.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even when things aren’t particularly stressful at work or home?

I don’t think so, not in a clear way. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, and there are days I feel worn out by trying to keep everything straight, but I wouldn’t say I’m just sad for no reason or not interested in things I normally care about.

At least… I don’t think that’s the main issue. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Can you describe if and how these difficulties with organization and prioritization show up in areas of your life outside of work, like with personal projects, social plans, or daily routines?

Yes, it does show up outside work too, although maybe not as dramatically. It’s more that I’ll have several personal things in my head at once, and instead of sorting out what actually needs to happen first, I sort of react to whatever feels most pressing right then.

So even with non-work things, I can get pulled into the loudest thing rather than the most important thing. I try to make lists and keep it under control, but the organizing part—the “what matters first, what comes next” part—has been harder than I’d like to admit. Does that make sense?
Have you noticed yourself getting more irritable or emotionally reactive than usual, even in situations that wouldn't have bothered you much before?

I’m not sure I’d say “more irritable,” exactly. I mean, everyone gets short sometimes, and I probably do get a bit tense when I’m trying to juggle too much, but I haven’t really noticed myself snapping at people in some new or extreme way.

Maybe I’m not the best judge of that, though. I can pay more attention to it if that would be helpful.
Have you noticed a decrease in your enjoyment or interest in activities that you used to find pleasurable, even when you're not particularly stressed?

I don’t think I’ve noticed that, no. If I’m not stressed, I can still enjoy the things I usually like.

Sometimes I don’t get around to them or I feel a little guilty that I should be doing something else, but the interest itself isn’t really gone. I hope that’s answering it the right way.

Can you describe how long you’ve been experiencing these difficulties with organization and prioritization? Have they been present for most of your life, or is this something that started more recently under increased stress?

I’d say it’s been a real problem for about a year or so… maybe a year and a month. It wasn’t like one day everything changed, but after I got that award and started being pulled into more coordination-heavy work, that’s when it became much more noticeable.

I don’t want to overstate it, because I’ve always had my own way of keeping things together, but this level of difficulty with figuring out what to prioritize and keeping it organized feels more recent. Does that distinction help?

Looking back, would you say that difficulties with staying organized, keeping track of tasks, and deciding what to do first have been a long-standing pattern for you, even going back to school or earlier, or is this something that’s mostly developed more recently?

Yeah… thinking about it more carefully, I guess there were signs of it pretty early on. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was, because I did fine in school overall, but I remember teachers saying things like I was bright, but I daydreamed a lot.

And there were definitely times I’d finish homework and then just… not turn it in, or I’d lose the folder it was in. That was back in grade school, before I was a teenager. So I guess it wasn’t completely new, even if it’s become more of a problem recently. Does that make sense?

Can you recall if these kinds of difficulties—like trouble staying focused, keeping track of things, or organizing tasks—used to show up in other parts of your life, like when you were in school or hanging out with friends, or have they mostly been a work-related issue?

I think it did show up outside of work, yes. Not in a dramatic way, or at least I didn’t think of it that way at the time, but looking back at school there were definitely comments from teachers that I was bright but daydreamed.

And I remember finishing assignments and then somehow not turning them in, or losing the folder with the homework in it. That was in grade school, so it was long before I was a teenager. I guess I tended to explain it away because I was doing okay overall, but it probably was there earlier than just work. Does that answer what you mean?

Can you describe any specific situations where these difficulties have caused noticeable problems—like missing an important deadline, struggling to complete a project, or conflicts with others because things weren’t organized or followed through on?

Yeah… there have been a couple of situations that were hard to ignore.

I don’t think I completely failed at them, but I did miss a patent filing checkpoint, and that was embarrassing because it reflected badly on my reliability. And there was a difficult architecture review where I wasn’t as organized or on top of the follow-through as I needed to be. After that, I got the sense that some collaborators were questioning whether I could really lead the larger project.

That’s probably the part that worries me most — it’s starting to affect how people see me at work, not just how stressed I feel internally. Does that answer the kind of example you mean?
Can you describe if you've had trouble focusing or staying attentive during everyday activities like reading, watching a movie, or having a conversation, not just when you're working on tasks?

Yeah, I mean… it’s not only formal work tasks. I wouldn’t say I can’t pay attention at all, but I do lose the thread pretty easily if something pulls at me.

Like if I’m coding and Slack pings, or a browser tab flashes, or even just some visual idea pops into my head, I can suddenly be off in a totally different direction. I’ll think I’m just checking one thing, and then twenty minutes later I’m down some unrelated design rabbit hole and I’ve forgotten exactly where I was.

So yes, I guess that kind of distractibility shows up outside of just “hard work,” too. Is that the sort of thing you mean?
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or like you need to be doing something constantly, even in situations where others might be more relaxed?

A bit, yeah. I wouldn’t say I’m bouncing off the walls or anything, but on long design calls I notice this pressure building, like I really need to move.

I’ll pace around my office if I’m off camera, or shift from one chair to another, even though I’m trying to look like I’m focused and settled. It’s not always obvious to other people, I hope, but internally it can feel pretty hard to just sit there calmly. Is that the kind of restlessness you mean?
Can you recall if you had trouble staying focused, keeping track of things, or organizing tasks before you turned 12, like during elementary school?

Yeah… looking back, I think it was there earlier than I probably admitted to myself.

I did fine in school overall, so it wasn’t like I was seen as a “problem kid,” but I remember teachers writing things like I was bright but daydreamed. And I’d sometimes finish assignments and then forget to actually turn them in, which sounds ridiculous, but it happened. I also lost homework folders more than I’d like to admit.

So yes, before middle school, definitely before I was 12, there were signs of the same kind of thing. Does that help answer it?
Do you find yourself often talking more than others in conversations, or interrupting people before they finish speaking?

Um… I don’t think that’s a big one for me, honestly. I mean, I can probably get enthusiastic and talk a lot if it’s something I care about, but I don’t think people would describe me as constantly interrupting or dominating conversations.

I try pretty hard to let people finish, maybe sometimes too hard because I’m aware of not wanting to come across that way. So… not really, at least not that I’ve noticed. Does that answer it?

target_item.manifestation: Looking back, this was there in grade school too—my teachers wrote that I was bright but daydreamed, forgot to turn in finished assignments, and lost homework folders long before I was a teenager.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these attention, tracking, and organization problems were present before age 12, which directly matches the onset-before-12 requirement.

patient.answer:
Yeah… looking back, I think it was there earlier than I probably admitted to myself.

I did fine in school overall, so it wasn’t like I was seen as a “problem kid,” but I remember teachers writing things like I was bright but daydreamed. And I’d sometimes finish assignments and then forget to actually turn them in, which sounds ridiculous, but it happened. I also lost homework folders more than I’d like to admit.

So yes, before middle school, definitely before I was 12, there were signs of the same kind of thing. Does that help answer it?

inference.note: This turn added F90.8 (Other childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and F90.9 (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, unspecified) as the patient's symptoms appear to have started before age 12 and are not limited to work settings, which supports a diagnosis related to ADHD. The symptoms described are broader than just ADHD combined presentation (F90.0), and the distinction between childhood-onset and unspecified became relevant based on developmental history.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient often talks excessively or interrupts others, which would support F90.0 or F90.8 over other candidates
doctor.question: Do you find yourself often talking more than others in conversations, or interrupting people before they finish speaking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive talking or interrupting others, but the provided symptom profile does not include an item covering those impulsive/conversational symptoms.

patient.answer:
Um… I don’t think that’s a big one for me, honestly. I mean, I can probably get enthusiastic and talk a lot if it’s something I care about, but I don’t think people would describe me as constantly interrupting or dominating conversations.

I try pretty hard to let people finish, maybe sometimes too hard because I’m aware of not wanting to come across that way. So… not really, at least not that I’ve noticed. Does that answer it?

inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including long-standing difficulties with organization, attention, and task prioritization dating back to childhood, along with current functional impairment in work and daily life, are most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation (F90.0). Other candidates (F48.0, F90.8, F90.9) are less supported based on the detailed developmental history and current symptom profile.
